generation.text: A familiar weather pattern is the rainstorm. The cause of rainstorms is when warm, moist air rises and cools in the atmosphere. As the air rises, it expands and cools, causing the water vapor in the air to condense into tiny droplets, forming clouds. When these droplets combine and become heavy, they fall as rain. The effect is a sudden increase in precipitation, often accompanied by wind and thunder. As the warm, moist air rises, it pushes out cooler, drier air, which can lead to changes in temperature and pressure. This can cause gusty winds and even tornadoes in some cases. The rain also provides water for plants and animals, replenishes groundwater, and can cause flooding if there is too much rain in a short period of time. Overall, rainstorms are a natural part of the water cycle
